These are the words which Moshe spoke unto all Yisrael. [The reference is] to the commandments which he will mention in the entire book beginning with the Ten Commandments in the section of Va’ethchanan,15Further 5:6-18. In other words, the opening expression of the Torah here, These are the words …, is not a reference to the words of Moshe from the beginning of the book on, narrating the historical events of the journey through the wilderness, but primarily a reference to the Ten Commandments and the laws that followed, which Moshe introduced with a review of their journey from Sinai to the Yarden followed with an exhortation to obedience. as Scripture stated, Moshe began explaining this Law, saying,16Verse 5. clearly indicating that he is speaking of the Law [which begins with the Ten Commandments in the next section of Va’ethchanan]. And in that case [we must say] that in the [following] verse Hashem our Elokim spoke unto us17Verse 6. an introductory expression of “saying.”18Since we have explained the word leimor (saying) in Verse 5 as referring not to the contents of Verse 6 but to the Scriptural text of the Ten Commandments, Verse 6 should begin with a phrase explaining that it was Moshe who was now speaking on a different subject — not about the commandments, but about the history of the forty years. Thus the verse should begin, “And he [i.e., Moshe] said: Hashem our Elokim spoke unto us …” is omitted. Similarly [there is an omission in the verse] And Yosef called the name of the firstborn Menashe: ‘for Elokim hath made me forget all my toil’ … And the name of the second he called Efraim: ‘for Elokim hath made me fruitful.’19Genesis 41:51-52. Both verses omit the expression “for he [Yosef] said” [that Elokim hath made me forget … “for he said” that Elokim hath made me fruitful]. And the purport of these verses here is as follows: “These are the commandments which Moshe spoke to all Yisrael beyond the Yarden in the fortieth year from their departure from Mitzrayim on the first day of the eleventh month according to all that Hashem had commanded him for them,20Verse 3. this being after he had smitten Sichon and Og,21Verse 4. in the land of Moav, there Moshe began to explain to them this Law, as follows. And he said: Hashem our Elokim spoke unto us in Chorev, saying: ‘Ye have dwelt long enough etc.’”17Verse 6. And the meaning thereof is that when Moshe began explaining the commandments to them, he said to them at the outset of his words: Hashem our Elokim spoke unto us in Chorev, after He gave us the Ten Commandments, [ordering] that we conquer the Land at once and that we cross the Yarden. But your sins caused you this and that consequence [as Moshe goes on to relate]. The words of this introduction continue until he concludes with the verse, And thou shalt keep His statutes, and His commandments, which I command thee this day, that it may go well with thee, and with thy children after thee, and that thou mayest prolong thy days upon the Land, which Hashem thy Elokim giveth thee, forever.22Further, 4:40. Then Moshe called all Yisrael that were before him and said, Hear, O Yisrael, the statutes and the ordinances which I speak in your ears this day,23Ibid., 5:1. and then began the explanation of the Torah with the Ten Commandments in order that they hear them with the explanation from the mouth of the one who received them from the mouth of the Holy One, blessed be He. Afterwards he informed them of the Unity of Elokim, as it is said, Hear, O Yisrael: Hashem our Elokim, Hashem is One,24Ibid., 6:4. and all the commandments in this book. This is why Scripture explained here which Moshe spoke unto ‘all’ Yisrael, and there it is stated, And Moshe called unto ‘all’ Yisrael23Ibid., 5:1. [emphasizing that all were present], because the explanation of the Torah and the completion of the commandments must be in the presence of “all” Yisrael just as was the Giving of the Torah [itself on Mount Sinai]. Now, because he [Moshe] prolonged the words of this introduction, Scripture [in Va’ethchanan where Moshe finally begins explaining “the words” with which he began this opening verse] returned to the place at which it stopped at the beginning of the explanation of the Torah and said, And this is the Law which Moshe set before the children of Yisrael; these are the testimonies, and the statutes, and the ordinances, which Moshe spoke unto the children of Yisrael, when they came forth out of Mitzrayim,25Ibid., 4:44-45. and mentioned that it was beyond the Yarden, in the valley over against Beit Peor, in the land of Sichon,26Ibid., Verse 46. this being the land of Moav mentioned here16Verse 5. since Yisrael did not enter the land of Moav except what was made permissible for them by Sichon [who conquered part of Moav and became its ruler, thus removing that territory from the injunction that Yisrael may not wage war against Moav] as has been explained in the preceding book.27Numbers 21:26; 35:14.
Thus Scripture mentioned two things here. [The first thing is:] it stated that Moshe spoke unto the children of Yisrael, according to all that Hashem had commanded him for them,20Verse 3. this being an allusion to the commandments which he would tell them in this book that have not been mentioned thus far in the Torah. And it says that these commandments were exactly as Elokim commanded him; he did not add to, or substract from what he had been commanded. It was necessary that this be stated [i.e., that Moshe spoke according to all that Hashem had commanded him] because Scripture does not state of them “And Hashem spoke unto Moshe;” therefore it included them now, [emphasizing] that they were all according to what he was commanded from the mouth of the Holy One, blessed be He. [The second thing is:] it further stated that Moshe began explaining this Law,16Verse 5. this being an allusion to the commandments which were already declared, that he would repeat them in order to clarify them further and to give additional instruction about them. And the meaning of the expression ho’il Mosheh28Verse 5. This is generally translated: “Moshe began.” Since according to Ramban, the explanation of the commandments does not begin until the Ten Commandments in 5:6, Ramban interprets the word ho’il as “wished;” thus meaning “Moshe wished” to explain this Torah; however, the beginning thereof is not here, but later on as explained. According to those commentators, such as Rashi, who explain the reference ‘These are the words’ in our verse as referring to Moshe’s words of chastisement, the word ho’il does mean “begin,” since the reproof begins in the next verse. is that “Moshe wished” to explain the Torah to them. This is said to inform us that Moshe saw fit to do so although Elokim had not yet commanded him thereon [but afterwards, when He commanded him to write down the whole Torah, Elokim Himself said all these words that were originally spoken by Moshe; and Moshe wrote them as he was commanded. Hence there is no difference between the first four books of the Torah and this fifth book, Deuteronomy, as all are equally the word of Elokim]. The word ho’il is thus related to the expressions: ‘ho’el na’ (be willing, I pray thee), and tarry all night;29Judges 19:6. would that ‘ho’alnu’ (we had been willing) and dwelt beyond the Yarden,30Yehoshua 7:7. and so also many similar expressions.

It is eleven days’ journey by the way of Seir unto Kadesh Barnea. The meaning thereof is that Scripture informs us of the vastness of the wilderness, that from Chorev, which they left, to Kadesh Barnea is a journey of only eleven days, since by way of Mount Seir it is near. Kadesh Barnea is at the end of the wilderness at the border of the hill-country of the Emori31Verse 7. which is the inheritance of Yisrael. There are the lands of Sichon and Og where Moshe explained the Torah in the valley over against Beit Peor.32Further, 4:46. Afterwards Scripture says, they went by way of the mountain of the Emori all that great and fearful wilderness,33Verse 19 (here). and, following that, it narrates that in Kadesh Barnea,33Verse 19 (here). which is at the boundary of their inheritance, they requested spies [to see the Land]. As a result, their journey was disrupted and they went [into the wilderness] toward the Red Sea34Verse 40. — backward and not forward35Yirmiyahu 7:24. — until the completion of forty years. And because Yisrael was presently not in the wilderness, since they had already entered the land of Moav, earlier mentioned [i.e., the part which they took from Sichon and Og], Onkelos interpreted the expression in the wilderness, in the plain [These are the words which Moshe spoke unto all Yisrael beyond the Yarden ‘in the wilderness, in the plain’]36Verse 1. as being allusions to reproof [thus rendering: he reproved them “on account of that which they provoked Him in the wilderness, etc.”]. Moreover, why should Scripture mention all these places [in the wilderness, in the plain, over against Suph, between Paran and Tofel, and Lavan, and Chatzerot, and Dizahab]36Verse 1. and specify signs and borders more than [the law requires] in selling a field! [Therefore these place-names were interpreted by Onkelos as being allusions to certain deeds about which Moshe reproved them.] And the sense of the Scripture according to Onkelos’ opinion is: “These are the words which Moshe spoke unto all Yisrael beyond the Yarden; he spoke of [that which they did] in the wilderness, in the plain, and over against Suph, between Paran and Tofel, and Lavan, and Chatzerot, and Di Zahav, and the eleven days’ journey from Chorev,” because he mentioned to them all that they had done in these places. Afterwards Scripture states that there, beyond the previously mentioned Yarden, Moshe wanted37See Ramban at the end of preceding verse, and Note 28. to explain the Torah after he reproved them, and he spoke and said, Hashem our Elokim spoke unto us in Chorev, saying.17Verse 6. And so it is interpreted in the Sifre38Sifre, Devarim 1. according to the opinion of Rabbi Yehudah. Rabbi Yosei ben Durmaskis, however, holds that they were actual places called by these names.

After he had smitten Sichon, the king of the Emori, who ‘dwelt’ in Cheshbon — for Cheshbon was not his, but he conquered it from the king of Moav and he built it to be his royal capital. Similarly, and Og the king of Bashan, who ‘dwelt’ in Ashtarot, at Edrei39In Verse 4 before us. means that it was previously the land of Refaim40Further, 3:13. [and then it was occupied by the king of the Emori] as I will explain41Ibid., 2:10; 3:11. with the help of Hashem. And because Scripture states, who dwelt in Ashtarot, at Edrei,39In Verse 4 before us. it indicates that Ashtarot is the name of a place in which Edrei is located [as will be explained further]. The text of the Sifre is as follows:42Sifre, Devarim 3. “‘B’ashtaroth’ — it was as hard as ashtaroth. ‘B’edrei’ — this was the seat of the government [i.e., the royal city].” Rashi wrote: “Ashtarot — is an expression denoting rocks and hardness. Ashtarot is Ashteroth-karnaim43Genesis 14:5. This is an expression for “strength” [“the hard rocks of Kamayim”]. where the Refaim were, as it is said, and they smote the Refaim in Ashteroth-karnaim.43Genesis 14:5. This is an expression for “strength” [“the hard rocks of Kamayim”]. ‘B’edrei’ — this was the name of the kingdom [indicating that the kingdom of Edrei was located in Ashteroth-karnaim]. And44The text from this point on, until the end of the quotation is not found in our texts of Rashi. Part of it is found in Rashi further, 7:13. so it is written, ‘ashteroth’ of thy sheep,45Further, 7:13. meaning, as Targum [Onkelos] rendered it [‘the flocks of thy sheep’]. And our Rabbis have said:46Chullin 84b. Why is the name ashtaroth given to them [i.e., flocks of sheep]? It is because they ‘enrich’ [from the Hebrew word ashir — rich] their owners and strengthen them like these ashtaroth which are strong rocks.” [This is Rashi’s language].
Now the Rabbi [Rashi] incorporated into the word [ashtaroth] two meanings [strength and riches], but we do not know from what source the Rabbi inferred that ashtaroth is a name for rocks and stones. But it is possible for us to say that ashtaroth is a term for flocks of sheep, from the word ashir (rich) as in the words of the Sages [quoted above: “Why is their name ashtaroth? It is because they enrich their owners”]. Ashteroth-karnaim43Genesis 14:5. This is an expression for “strength” [“the hard rocks of Kamayim”]. was a place of high mountains upon which there were strongholds of stone, these being likened by Scripture to “the horns of cattle,” just as Scripture likens them to “teeth,” as it says upon ‘the crag’ [literally: “the tooth”] of the rock, and the stronghold.47Iyov 39:28. Similarly, upon ‘the horns’ of the altar.48Exodus 29:12. So also, ‘b’keren’ ben shamen49Yeshayahu 5:1. These verses illustrate the Scriptural tendency of likening topographical characteristics to parts of animals such as horns and teeth. [literally: “in a fruitful ‘horn'”] which the Targum [Yonathan ben Uziel] renders: “On a high hill, in a fruitful land.” There, [upon these high hills,] the flocks of sheep ascend, the he-goats, the she-goats, and the wild-goats50Psalms 104:18: The high mountains are for the wild-goats. and their like; and therefore the place is called Ashteroth-karnaim51Judges 2:13. [because the flocks which “enrich” their owners (ashtaroth) ascend to the “horns” of the mountain (karnaim)]. So also, and they served Ba'al and the Ashtarot51Judges 2:13. — ‘Ashtarot’ because the idol was made in the form of a sheep in order to protect them [the flocks of sheep], in accordance with their foolish belief. [This is in line with our explanation of the word ashtaroth as a synonym for sheep.] Now at the foot of the mountain they built a city whose name was Edrei, this being intimated in the verse which states, and Og the king of Bashan came out against us, he and all his people, unto battle at Edrei,52Further, 3:1. This verse clearly indicates that Edrei is the name of a particular locality rather than the name of the entire country, hence it can be said that Og gathered his army there. This proves Ramban’s explanation “that Ashtarot is the name of a region wherein Edrei is located.” However, it could not be as Rashi explained that Edrei is the name of the kingdom, for if it were the name of an entire country, how could it be said that Og, gathered his army “at Edrei” when it is not the name of a specific, particular place? (Aboab). denoting that he gathered his entire army to the city where the palace of the king and the throne of the kingdom were. And this is the purport of the [following] Midrashic text [which seems to agree with Rashi’s interpretation], wherein the Rabbis, of blessed memory, have stated: “Who dwelt in Ashtarot, at Edrei. Even if Og himself had not been difficult to defeat but had resided in Ashtarot, he would have been difficult to defeat, because the city was a difficult one to capture etc.”53“And even if the city had not been difficult to capture, but Og resided in it, it would have been difficult to capture because its king was difficult to defeat. How much more so when the king was difficult to defeat and the city difficult to capture” (Sifre). Therefore they interpreted, Ashtarot to mean that it was “as hard as Ashtarot,”54In other words, the word Ashtarot here does not indicate something hard. But because Og’s royal city Edrei was well fortified, the Sifre compares it to Ashteroth-karnaim where the Refaim lived and from where Og originated. [the phrase from which Rashi, quoted above, deduced that the word ashtaroth is defined as “hard”], as if to say that his residence was like the fortified city of Ashteroth-karnaim43Genesis 14:5. This is an expression for “strength” [“the hard rocks of Kamayim”]. from which he and his family originated; for at that time he was not residing in Ashtarot, but was residing in the land of the Emori. And “the place of the government” [mentioned in the Sifre above] means that the city where he lived was Edrei55Thus, unlike Rashi who wrote that Edrei was the name of the kingdom, Ramban holds that Edrei was the name of the royal city, and the name of the kingdom was “The Bashan.” but Bashan was the name of the land of his kingdom.

Hashem our Elokim spoke unto us in Chorev, saying. In my opinion Chorev was the name of a place near Mount Sinai56See Vol. II, pp. 239, 253. where Yisrael dwelled in the year [of the exodus]. The wilderness was large and therein was the mountain which Elokim hath desired;57Psalms 68:17. its name was Sinai and it is for this reason that the entire wilderness is called the wilderness of Sinai,58Exodus 19:1. as it were, “the wilderness of Mount Sinai.” Thus Scripture states, and they came to the wilderness of Sinai, and they encamped in the wilderness; and there Yisrael encamped opposite the mount,59Ibid., Verse 2. meaning that they encamped in the wilderness in a place called Chorev, this being opposite the mountain. It is possible that both the mountain and the wilderness were called “Sinai” because many sneh (thorn-bush) trees were there, and near that mountain was a locality or an inhabited city called Chorev, and there they stopped. And the verse which states, and he [Moshe] came to the mountain of Elokim, unto Chorev60Ibid., 3:1. [which might indicate that the name of the mountain itself was really Chorev or, perhaps, that the mountain was in the region called Chorev], means that he came to Chorev where the mountain of Elokim was. Now the sneh (thorn-bush) [out of the midst of which the angel appeared to Moshe] was on that mountain. Moshe [at that moment] was in Chorev, the place before it, nearby, where the camp of Yisrael stood for [close to] a year [after the exodus]. Therefore Moshe said, I will turn aside now and see [this great sight, why is the bush not consumed],61Ibid., Verse 3. meaning that he will turn aside from Chorev [and walk] up to the mountain. At times Scripture calls the mountain itself [Chorev], as it is said, And the children of Yisrael stripped themselves of their ornaments from Mount Chorev,62Ibid., 33:6. that is to say “from the mountain which was in the area of Chorev, in its vicinity or before it.” Or it may be that Chorev was the name of the entire region and the mountain was within it. Similarly, Remember ye the law of Moshe My servant, which I commanded unto him in Chorev for all Yisrael, even statutes and ordinances,63Malachi 3:22. alludes to all that he was commanded on the mountain, and in the Tent of Meeting which was there in Chorev.
Now I have seen a Midrash in Yelamdeinu Rabbeinu:64Literally: “May our master teach us.” See Vol. II, p. 131, Note 196, for description of this Midrash. “Yea, thou knewest not65Yeshayahu 48:8. The verse reads: Yea, thou heardest not; yea thou knewest not; yea, from of old … — at Sinai; yea, thou heardest not — at Chorev; yea, from of old thine ear was not opened — in the plains of Moav.” The Midrash thus intimates that Chorev is the place where the Tent of Meeting was, [thus confirming the view that Sinai and Chorev are different places]. However, Rabbi Avraham ibn Ezra states66Choreb in Hebrew means “desolation,” or “dryness.” — This interpretation is found in Ibn Ezra’s commentary to Exodus 3:1-2. that Chorev is Mount Sinai, for, because of its desolation and dryness, the sneh (thorn-bush) grows there, so the mountain is known by two names [Chorev and Sinai], both being similar in meaning [“Chorev” referring to its desolate nature, and “Sinai” indicating the thorn-bushes that are products of the dryness].

Turn you, and take your journey, and go to the Mount of the AMORITE etc. He mentioned to them the Land and the road that they are to traverse in their stages, and afterwards He said, Behold, I have set the Land before you which I swore to your fathers; go in and possess the Land67Verse 8. — this being a command, not just an assurance and promise, as I have explained.68Numbers 33:53, Ramban thus reiterates here his theory that the precept to conquer the Land of Yisrael is included in Taryag (six hundred and thirteen) mitzvoth which are binding for all times; that we are not to leave it in the hands of other nations, that we are not to leave it to waste, and that we are to dwell in it. See more fully in Vol. IV, pp. 385-386.

Which Hashem swore. The reason [for using the third person Hashem swore rather than the first person “I swore” which would be more appropriate, since Hashem is the speaker] is similar to that in the verse, And unto Moshe He said, Come up to Hashem,69Exodus 24:1. [rather than “Come up unto Me”]. There I have explained it.70See ibid., Vol. II, pp. 422-424.

And I spoke unto you at that time, saying: ‘I am not able to bear you myself alone.’ [Moshe’s statement here in this verse was actually said] before Hashem said to us in Chorev, Ye have dwelt long enough in this mountain,71Above, Verse 6. For, according to the opinion that Yitro came before the Giving of the Torah, the appointment of judges (recorded here in the following verses) took place almost a year before they moved away from Chorev. Hence we must say that the whole episode that begins with Verse 9 happened before Yisrael was commanded to journey from Chorev (Verse 6). And the expression at that time (in this verse) means “while we dwelled at Chorev.” But according to the Sages who say that Yitro came after the Giving of the Torah, the expression at that time means “at that time when we were about to leave Chorev.” according to the opinion of those who say that Yitro came before the Giving of the Torah.72See Exodus 18:1; Vol. II, pp. 249-252. And the meaning of the expression at that time [in the verse before us] is “while we dwelled at Chorev.” But Moshe mentioned it here [in Verse 9, rather than before Verse 6] to convey the following thought: We received the Torah, and you had judges and officers to judge you and lead you, and we were thus ready to enter the Land. And we journeyed from Chorev73Further, Verse 19, and Verse 22. in our [four] divisions with our judges and our elders, and then ye came near unto me every one of you73Further, Verse 19, and Verse 22. with your wise men and your leaders and you wanted spies to be sent, and thus the plan [for an immediate entry into the Land] was frustrated.

How can I myself alone bear ‘torchachem’ (your trouble) ‘umasa’achem’ (and your burden), v’rivchem (and your strife)? According to the simple meaning of Scripture, Moshe our teacher alluded to them the three things which he told Yitro that he was doing for the people, as I have explained there.74Exodus 18:15. Vol. II, p. 263. He now mentioned them to Yisrael by implication. He said torchachem corresponding to and I make known to them the statutes of Elokim and His laws,75Ibid., Verse 16. for it was a difficult “task” to teach those who had come forth from Mitzrayim, the statutes and the laws of Elokim, their meanings, interpretations, and secrets. He said masa’achem corresponding to the people come unto me to inquire of Hashem,74Exodus 18:15. Vol. II, p. 263. a reference to prayer, for he used to pray on their behalf. The word masa’achem is related to the expression: ‘v’nasatha t’filah’ (and thou lift up prayer);76II Kings 19:4. nor ‘tisa’ (lift up) entreaty or prayer in their behalf.77Yirmiyahu 7:16. [He stated] ‘v’rivchem’ (and your strife) which is to be understood in its plain sense — matters of judgments [because judges must rule when there is strife among people]. Moshe continued to state: Get you men who are wise, and understanding, and known among your tribes78Verse 13. — referring only to [the qualities of] judges. But he said unqualifiedly, and I will make them heads over you78Verse 13. by way of humility.79That is, Moshe told the people that he will make these judges “heads” over them — in all three of the above capacities: teaching, praying and judging. Actually, however, the “heads” were only for rendering judgment in matters of litigation between them, but not for teaching the statutes and the laws to the people, nor for praying on their behalf, those vital functions being the province of Moshe. Yet Moshe by way of humility said that he would appoint them to all three functions.
Now Rashi quotes from the Sifre:80Sifre, Devarim 12. “‘Torchachem’ (Your trouble). This teaches that they were troublesome. If one perceived that his opponent was winning a litigation, he would say ‘I have witnesses to bring; I have evidence to present; I [exercise my right to] add judges to you [thereby increasing the size of the court].’” But I do not know [the validity of] this law that one of the litigants should have the right to add judges above [the usual number of] three in cases concerning monetary matters, and surely he has no such right after presenting his case before them and perceiving that his opponent was winning the case! For, had he voluntarily accepted upon himself a relative or an unqualified person as a judge, he could indeed retract81Sanhedrin 31b. prior to the rendering of the final judgment, but from those qualified to judge he cannot retract [his acceptance]! Perhaps we can deduce from here the principle that a man can say, “I choose two judges and you choose two other ones, and they [i.e., the four judges] will choose one more,82For “a court must not be divisible evenly;” it must have an odd number of judges to assure that, in the event of a split, there would not be a tie vote (ibid., 2a). and let the suit be decided by five or more judges,” just as the Rabbis have said:83The precise source of this statement is unknown to me. Rambam states the thought as follows: “Although a court of three judges is a perfect tribunal, yet if they are more, it is to be praised” (Mishneh Torah, Hilchoth Sanhedrin 2:13). “A suit decided by five [judges] is not comparable to one decided by ten [judges].” Although three judges [have the power to] compel parties to come before them for judgment when one refuses to be bound by their decision, yet if one [of the litigants] desires to choose additional judges, he may do so, because it is similar to [the case of] one [of the litigants] who says, “Let us go to the main meeting place of the scholars [to bring our suit before them on the assumption that superior scholars are better qualified to judge],”81Sanhedrin 31b. in which case we accede to him, provided it does not entail [undue] hardship, for in such a case we have been commanded, Justice, justice, shalt thou pursue,84Further, 16:20. [which the Sifre interpreted]: “Go to a reliable court,” and an increase in the number constitutes “a reliable court.”85Sifre, Shoftim 144; Sanhedrin 32b. Now in the wilderness, wise men were available to them and the litigants could say, “Let us go before the officers of the thousands.”

Vidu’im l’shivteichem’ (and known among your tribes) — “men who are known to you. For if he were to come before me [Moshe] wrapped in his robe, I would not know who he is and of what tribe he is, but you know him for you have raised him.” This is Rashi’s language quoting the Sifre.86Sifre, Devarim 13. And if so, ‘l’shivteichem’ (among your tribes) is connected with the word ‘vidu’im’ (and known).87The Scriptural text [in the order of the words] reads: Get you men who are wise, and understanding, ‘vidu’im’ (and known) ‘l’shivteichem’ [literally: “‘to’ or ‘from’ each of your tribes”]. Now Rashi, on the basis of the Sifre, connects the last two words — “known to your tribes.” Ramban will explain l’shivteichem as referring to the first part of the verse: “Get you … from each of your tribes” and the word vidu’im he will explain as meaning and known to be judges and being qualified. But in line with the plain meaning of Scripture the purport of the verse is as follows: “Get you, from each of your tribes wise men.”86Sifre, Devarim 13. And the meaning of the word vidu’im in my opinion is that “they are known as judges,” that is to say, their capability is known and recognized as qualifying them to be appointed judges. Now [Moshe] epitomized the qualities of the judges in the word vidu’im, because the judges need to be able men, such as fear Elokim; men of truth, hating unjust gain,88Exodus 18:21. as Yitro said. And these men [that were appointed] were known from the beginning to be judges, for everyone was saying, “This one is fit to be a judge.”

For the judgment is Elokim’s. The meaning thereof is as expressed in the verse, for ye judge not for man, but for Hashem; and He is with you in giving judgment,89II Chronicles 19:6. These were the words of Yehoshafat, king of Yehudah, to the newly appointed judges. meaning to say: “It is for Elokim to execute justice between His creatures for He created them with the intention that there be fairness and justice among them, and to deliver him that is robbed out of the hand of the oppressor,90Yirmiyahu 22:3. and He designated you [the judges] in His stead. And if you will be afraid and act corruptly ye have sinned against Hashem91Numbers 32:23. and you will have betrayed His mission.”

And I commanded you at that time all the things which ye should do. “These are the ten differences between monetary and capital cases.” This is Rashi’s language quoting the Sifre.92Sifre, Devarim 18. See Sanhedrin 32a for these ten distinctions between monetary and capital cases. And if so, Moshe is speaking here to the judges [previously] mentioned, and he abridged on the ten differences [by not enumerating them], for they are all deduced from verses.
And in line with the plain meaning of Scripture, the reference here is to the statutes and laws, the way wherein they must walk, and the deeds they must perform,93Exodus 18:20. for he [Moshe] personally commanded, warned, and taught Yisrael all these matters. And the reason for mentioning this [subject] here is because it is known that this was the substance of Yitro’s counsel when he told Moshe, Be thou for the people before Elokim,94Ibid., Verse 19. meaning that he was to pray in their behalf in the time of their affliction, and he further told him, And thou shalt teach them the statutes and the laws etc.,93Exodus 18:20. meaning that he, himself, was to teach them the Torah. But regarding the execution of the law, Yitro advised him to appoint judges to assist him, and I have already explained it there.93Exodus 18:20. Therefore, Moshe related here that when he designated the officers over thousands and hundreds he delegated them only over the execution of justice. He, however, would personally teach them [the people] everything they were to do in accordance with the Torah, because he hearkened to his father-in-law’s counsel and did all that he had said.95Ibid., Verse 24. Now Moshe did not mention Yitro’s advice here, nor did he attribute to him anything that Yitro proposed. It appears to me that Moshe did not want to mention it [the fact that he was following his father-in-law’s advice] in the presence of all Yisrael because of his humility,96For people would think that, were it not for Yitro’s counsel, Moshe would not have needed any assistance from the other judges. But would he have brought in Yitro’s name into this affair it might have appeared that Moshe himself never thought that he would need assistance of other people. Moshe humility is thus made apparent when he states his own inability to cope with all the problems of the people (Keseph Mezukak). See further in my Hebrew commentary p. 349. or it may be that it would not be to his honor to mention to that generation that he had married a Kushi woman.97Numbers 12:1. — Since in the case of Zimri the son of Salu they chided Moshe about the Kushi woman [that he had married before the Torah was given — see Rashi, Numbers 25:6], he therefore avoided referring to it in order to prevent them from stumbling into evil speech (see my Hebrew commentary, p. 533). It is also possible that the reason [for not mentioning Yitro’s name] was because he had consulted the Divine Glory and this matter was done at the command of the Almighty.98Mechilta, Yithro 2: “And Moshe hearkened to the voice of his father-in-law and did all that ‘amar’ (he, [i.e. Elokim] had said” Exodus 18:24). The Mechilta thus explains the word amar as referring to Elokim, and not to Yitro.

And bring us back word of the way by which we must go up. “There is no road which does not have crooked segments. AND THE CITIES UNTO WHICH WE SHALL COME — first to capture.” This is Rashi’s language. And so it is also stated in the Sifre:99Sifre, Devarim 20. “There is no road which does not have crooked parts. There is no road which does not have traps. There is no road which does not have intersections. And the cities unto which we shall come — so that we may know by which road to come.” That is to say, from which direction we are to come into the Land so that we may capture those cities first. This is as I explained in the section Shelach Lecha100Numbers, at the beginning of Chapter 13. that Bnei Yisrael requested spies only to show them the way.

And I took twelve men of you. He did not praise them as being princes [of their tribes]101Ibid., Verse 2. and their being leaders of the children of Yisrael,102Ibid., Verse 3. for, since they acted wickedly, he would not speak in praise of wicked men.

And they said: ‘good is the land which Hashem our Elokim giveth unto us.’ “Who were those who spoke well of the Land? Yehoshua and Kalev.” This is Rashi’s language quoting the Sifre.103Sifre, Devarim 23. But I wonder. If so, what is this complaint against them [the people]? It was proper that they should believe ten people more than two? Perhaps Moshe complained against them: “Since the Holy One, blessed be He, had informed you that it is a good Land, and the leading emissaries and the most righteous among them had also testified to that effect, you should have believed that the others spoke their piece out of lack of courage.”
The correct interpretation is as I have already explained there:104Numbers 13:32. All the spies admitted before Moshe and Aharon and the whole congregation, saying, We came unto the Land whither thou sentest us, and surely it floweth with milk and honey; and this is the fruit of it.105Ibid., Verse 27. Thus they were all in consensus on the goodness of the Land itself, but, with reference to the strength of those nations living there, they melted the people’s hearts. Then, when [the ten spies] saw that Yehoshua and Kalev were encouraging the people to wage war, the spies came to the children of Yisrael not in the presence of Moshe and they disseminated a slanderous report about the Land to the effect that it is a Land that eateth up the inhabitants thereof.104Numbers 13:32. This is [what Moshe meant when he stated here], and ye murmured in your tents.106Verse 27 here. The expression in your tents clearly indicates that the murmuring was done surreptitiously. The ten wicked spies did not confront Moshe with this charge. The people also did not mention this slander in the presence of Moshe107In Verse 28, where Moshe quotes the words of the people’s complaint. for he would refute them because they [the spies themselves] did not say so at first [that the Land kills its inhabitants]; instead they admitted that it is a good Land, and surely it floweth with milk and honey.105Ibid., Verse 27. Rather, they said to Moshe, Whither are we going up? our brethren have made our heart to melt, saying: The people is greater and taller than we.107In Verse 28, where Moshe quotes the words of the people’s complaint. Therefore, Moshe now said to them: “It is true as you say that that people is great and tall, but Hashem will fight for you108Exodus 14:14. according to all that He did for you109Verse 30 here. from Mitzrayim even till now.”110Numbers 14:19. This, then, is the sense of the verse, Yet in this thing ye do not believe Hashem your Elokim,111Verse 32 here. which means that the hindrance [to your immediate entry into the Land] was only a result of insufficient faith [you had in Elokim]. Thus the whole section is explained in accordance with the simple meaning of Scripture and its purport.

Also Hashem was angry with me, for your sakes. He is stating: “Behold, the sin you committed then in the affair of the spies withheld from you the good Land, and yet you continued to sin another time [i.e., at the waters of Merivah] until you prevented me as well, from crossing [the Yarden].” For Moshe wanted to mention simultaneously that the punishment of all who were prevented from passing into the Land, was caused by their sins. Also in order to mention here the matter of Yehoshua,112Verse 38 here. that he would cross over because he followed Hashem wholeheartedly as did his colleague [Kalev],113Numbers 14:24. and, therefore, he will yet deserve to cause the second generation to inherit the Land, because Moshe was punished and it was decreed upon him that he was not to cross [the Yarden]. Thus Moshe mentioned the whole affair [of the spies] except for the death by plague of the spies themselves.114Ibid., Verse 37. Nor did he mention the slander [of the spies that the Land eateth up the inhabitants thereof],104Numbers 13:32. for he would not speak of the shame of individuals. Instead he reproved the multitude all of whom sinned and all of whom were punished.
The meaning of the expression for your sakes [Also Hashem was angry with me, ‘for your sakes’] is that the children of Yisrael strove with Hashem etc.115Ibid., 20:13. [at the waters of Merivah], and all this happened because of your quarrel. Or [the expression for your sakes] may allude to the fact that the anger [of Hashem] with Moshe and Aharon was because — when they hit the rock twice116Ibid., Verse 11. in front of the people [instead of speaking to it] and did not do as they were commanded — the people were critical of it.117See Ramban ibid., Verse 1 (towards end). This is the purport of His words, because ye sanctified Me not in the midst of the children of Yisrael,118Further, 32:51. meaning that the punishment came [not because the sin itself was so grievous, but] because it happened in the midst of the children of Yisrael that the Glory was not sanctified before their eyes. Thus the Rabbis have also said in the Sifre:119Sifre, Ha’azinu 340. “Because ye trespassed against Me.118Further, 32:51. — you caused [the people] to trespass. Because ye sanctified Me not118Further, 32:51. — you caused that I not be sanctified. Because ye rebelled against My commandment120Numbers 27:14. — you caused [the people] to rebel against My commandment.” The Rabbis [in the Sifre] thus interpreted all these expressions as transitional to Yisrael, [meaning, Moshe and Aharon had really not sinned in the affair of the rock, but since their action was misconstrued by the people causing the people to sin, Moshe and Aharon were punished]. I have already explained the subject.117See Ramban ibid., Verse 1 (towards end).

Anachnu’ (we) ‘na’aleh’ (we will go up) and fight. The purport of the word ‘anachnu’ (we) [when it is already included in the word na’aleh which means “we will go up”] is that “we ourselves” will go up and we will fight, and we will not leave the matter to our children after us, as you [Moshe] have said.

And ye returned and wept before Hashem. There [in the Book of Numbers]121Ibid., 14:45. Scripture did not mention this weeping, for there was no need to mention it. But Moshe mentioned it now as praise that they regretted their sin, and to tell them that this sin was too great to forgive122See Genesis 4:13. because the great oath [of Hashem] had already been pronounced, and a Heavenly decree accompanied by an oath cannot be rent.123Rosh Hashanah 18a.

Your brethren the children of Esav. The reason for this expression is that descent of Yisrael is from Avraham and all his seed are thus “brothers” because they were all circumcised. This is the purport of the verse, Thou shalt not abhor an Edomi, for he is ‘thy brother.’124Further, 23:8. Only the sons of the concubines125Genesis 25:6. [of Avraham], Yishmael, Midyan126Ibid., Verse 2. and all children of Keturah127Ibid., Verses 1-4. are not in this “brotherhood,” as we see from the verse, for in Yitzchak shall seed be called to thee.128Ibid., 21:12. Thus Esav [Edom] is in this “brotherhood” for he is a son of Yitzchak, but Yishmael, born of Hagar and Midyan, born of Keturah, although they are Avraham’s biological sons, are not in this “brotherhood,” for as G-d said to Avraham: in Yitzchak shall seed be called to thee. This makes it clear that the spiritual brotherhood of the Abrahamitic seed is restricted to descendants of Yitzchak. See my Hebrew commentary p. 351.

Ye shall purchase food of them for money. If you should desire to eat of the fruits of their land you should not take it from them except for the full price129Ibid., 23:9. at their pleasure, this being the sense of the word me’itam (of them) [purchase food ‘of them,’ i.e., with their consent]. Also you shall not drink water of them at all, except for money with their consent.

For Hashem thy Elokim hath blessed thee. “Therefore, you should not deny His goodness by behaving as though you were poor; instead deport yourselves like rich people.” This is Rashi’s language. Now, I have not understood what he meant [by the next phrase in the verse, For Hashem thy Elokim hath blessed thee] in all the work of thy hand, since their blessings were heavenly blessings and they did nothing with their hands that it be blessed! Perhaps the expression in all the work of thy hand alludes to the sheep and herds which they brought out from Mitzrayim.130Exodus 12:32. They also had riches, herds, and acquisitions from the spoils of the Mitzrim and the spoils of Amalek. Everything they possessed was blessed, similar to what is stated, Thou hast blessed the work of his hands, and his possessions are increased in the land.131Iyov 1:10. Moreover, Hashem hath known thy walking through this vast wilderness and He supplied you there with all your needs — the manna, the quails, and the waters of the well — so that thou hast lacked nothing that is needed by wayfarers. And so it was — they bought food and nourishment from the children of Esav as Moshe said [to Sichon], Thou shalt sell me food for money that I may eat, and give me water for money, that I may drink etc.; as the children of Esav did unto me etc.132Further, Verses 28-29.

The Eimim abode therein FORMERLY etc. “You [Moshe] might think that this is the land of the Refaim which I gave to Avraham133Genesis 15:20. because the Eimim, who are Refaim, dwelled there formerly, but this [the land of the Moavim] is not the land [that I promised to Avraham], because I drove out those Refaim from before the children of Lot and settled them in place of the Refaim. Those Eimim were considered Refaim,134In our texts of Rashi this is marked as a comment upon Verse 11: “They also were accounted Refaim, even as the Anakim (giants).” This is interpreted by Rashi to mean: “The Eimim who formerly lived in the lands of Amon and Moav were accounted as Refaim, that is, the Anakim, (giants). But those lands of Amon and Moav were not the land of the Refaim which I promised to Avraham.” Therefore Moshe was not to wage war against the lands of Amon and Moav. like Anakim (giants) who are called Refaim [from the root raphoh — weak] because the hands of everyone who sees them become ‘weak.’ Eimim [from the root eimah — fear] are so called because their ‘dread’ lays upon people.” This is Rashi’s language. And similarly he wrote [further, in connection with the land of Amon of which Scripture states], That also is accounted a land of Refaim:135Further, Verse 20. “because the Refaim dwelled there formerly, but that [land] is not what I gave to Avraham.”
But I wonder at the words of the Rabbi! Why should Scripture explain to us concerning the land of Amon and Moav that it is not the land of Refaim which He gave to Avraham? Was it to state that it was not due to Yisrael and was not part of the land which G-d swore to their fathers to give them? [That could not be the reason! On the contrary,] Scripture states only, because I have given it unto the children of Lot for a possession136Verse 19. meaning that, although it was part of Avraham’s inheritance, the Holy One, blessed be He, gave it to the children of Lot for Avraham’s sake. As Rashi himself wrote:137Here on Verse 5. “[The lands of] two nations [from among the ten nations originally given to Avraham — Genesis 15:19-21], I gave to the children of Lot [Amon and Moav] as a reward because Lot went with Avraham to Mitzrayim138Genesis 13:1. and kept silent concerning what Avraham said about his wife, ‘she is my sister.’” Moreover, the Rabbi himself wrote with reference to Esav:137Here on Verse 5. “[The lands of] ten nations139Ibid., 15:19-21: the Keini, and the Knizi, and the Kadmonite; and the Chiti, and the Perizi, and the Refaim; and the Emori, and the Kenaani, and the Girgashite, and the Yevusi. I gave to Avraham. Seven of them will be yours. [Concerning the lands of] the Keini, and the Knizi, and the Kadmonite — which are Amon and Moav, and Mount Seir — one [i.e., Mount Seir] belongs to Esav, and two of them to the children of Lot.” And if so, the lands of Amon and Moav, and Mount Seir were certainly of the inheritance of Avraham; why then did the Holy One, blessed be He, say to Moshe that he should not think that this [land of Amon and Moav] is the land of Refaim which was given to Avraham? What difference is there between [the lands of] the Keini, and the Knizi, and the Kadmonite [which were promised to Avraham but given to the children of Lot and Esav], and [the land of] the Refaim [which was also promised to Avraham]?140In other words, Rashi wrote of the lands of the Keini, etc., that, notwithstanding the fact that they were of the inheritance of Avraham, they were still given to the children of Lot for the reason stated by Rashi that Lot protected Avraham’s secret in Mitzrayim. Similarly we could say that the land of the Refaim, too, was originally destined for Avraham, but that G-d gave it to another nation. Therefore, on what does Rashi base his assertion that this land was not the land of Refaim promised to Avraham? Moreover, the expression Refaim dwelled there ‘l’phanim’ (of old)135Further, Verse 20. indicates that it belongs to them because they dwelled there before anyone else, as in the verse ‘l’phanim’ (of old) Thou didst lay the foundation of the earth141Psalms 102:26. [thus raising another question on Rashi’s assertion: If the Refaim lived there “of old,” why was this land given to the children of Lot]?
But the interpretation of the verses is the opposite of the Rabbi’s [Rashi’s] words. It was because the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moshe, Be not at enmity with Moav etc. because I have given Ar unto the children of Lot for a possession,142Verse 9. Scripture tells that the land was indeed due to the seed of Avraham except that He gave it to the children of Lot. Scripture further says that in that land there dwelled of old a people great, and many, and tall, as the Anakim,143Verse 10 before us. and, therefore, the Moavim called them ‘Eimim’144Verse 11. because of the great “dread” which they cast upon those who saw them. Now G-d, in honor of Avraham, performed a miracle for the children of Lot. They defeated [the Eimim] and drove them from before them; it is therefore not proper to take from them by force the land which G-d gave them through a miracle. ‘Yeichashvu’ [They were also ‘yeichashvu’ Refaim]144Verse 11. is an expression of importance and esteem, similar to the following: he was despised, and we did not ‘chashavnuhu’ (esteem him);145Yeshayahu 53:3. who shall not ‘yachshovu’ (regard) silver?;146Ibid., 13:17. for how little is he ‘nechshav’ (esteemed)?147Ibid., 2:22. and so many others. And in the language of the Sages we find the expression adam chashuv (an esteemed person).148Berachoth 19a.
This is why Scripture placed the statements in proximity to [the verse that discussed the lands of Amon and Moav, the children of Lot]. And in Seir the Horim abode formerly.149Verse 12. It declares that for the same reason He stated [for restraining Yisrael from attacking] Moav, He likewise withheld them [Yisrael] from attacking the land of Seir. Because formerly it also belonged to the Horim, and it was part of the gift to Avraham — for the Chori is identical with the Chivi, and they [the Chivi] were of the children of Kenaan, as it is said, Esav took his wives of the daughters of ‘Kenaan’ etc. and Oholivamah the daughter of Anah, the daughter of Tzivon ‘the Chivi’150Genesis 36:1. and Tzivon was of the sons of Seir ‘the Chori,’ the inhabitants of the land.151Ibid., Verse 20. So, also, wherever the inheritance of Yisrael is mentioned, the Chivi is always included with the Kenaani among the seven nations,152See further, 7:1, etc. because the Chivi is enumerated as the sixth son among the children of Kenaan.153See Genesis 10:17. You will also see this in the narrative of the war of Amrafel which he fought against the kings of Sedom, Amorah, Admah, Zebaiim, and Tzoar,154See ibid., 14:8-9. who were Kenaani kings. They [Amrafel and his associates] smote ‘the Rephaiim’ in Ashteroth-karnaim,155Ibid., Verse 5. and ‘the Chori’ in their mountain, Seir,156Ibid., Verse 6. for the Chori and the Refaim belonged to the Kenaani kings.
It is possible that [the Chori] was called Chivi [from the term chivi — a snake] because he was like a serpent in the way.157Ibid., 49:17. He was also called the Chori from the noun ‘chor’ (the hole of) the asp.158Yeshayahu 11:8. For names [like Chori, Chivi] preserve the meaning and change letters, like Zerach (Zerach)159Numbers 26:13. The Hebrew word Zerach means “shining.” and Tzochar (Zohar),160Exodus 6:15. Tzochar and Zerach both are names for the same son of Shimon. of the expression: and ‘tzochar’ (white) wool;161Yechezkel 27:18. ‘tzchoroth’ (white) asses,162Judges 5:10. Ramban thus shows that the names Zerach and Tzochar (from the words “shining” and “white”) both refer to the same person although the letters in the names interchange. [and in the case of the Chori and Chivi, the names were chosen to suggest the treacherous, snake-like nature of the people]. They also assign new names to praise [someone]. Thus the name Ya’akov (Yaakov), an expression of guile or of deviousness,163Genesis 27:36. — Ibid., 32:29 [Yaakov’s name changed to Yisrael]. was changed to Yisrael [from the word sar (prince)] and they called him Yeshurun (Yeshurun)164Further, 32:15. from the expression whole-hearted ‘v’yashar’ (and upright).165Iyov 1:1.
Thus Scripture is stating that the Chori [whose land was] given to Avraham166Since the Chori are identical with the Chivi, as explained above, and the Chivi were children of Kenaan, and the Kenaani is among the ten nations whose lands were given to Avraham (Genesis 15:21), it follows that the land of the Chori was given to Avraham. dwelled formerly in Seir, and the children of Esav who are of the seed of Avraham succeeded them and dwelled in their stead by a miraculous event. The Chori were a populous nation in their land and the children of Esav came to dwell there and overpowered them just as Yisrael did to the remaining nations [in the land that was] promised to Avraham, that G-d gave them in His great power. Thus G-d divided [the lands of] all these [ten] nations among the seed of Avraham — one to Esav, and the balance to Yisrael who was the firstborn son.167See Exodus 4:22. It is therefore not proper to steal from Esav what G-d caused him to inherit, since G-d would be angry with anyone who would forcibly take from him [Esav] the inheritance that He, blessed be He, caused him to inherit, just as He would be wroth with him who would forcibly take the Land from Yisrael after He caused him [Yisrael] to inherit it, just as it says, As for all Mine evil neighbors, that touch the inheritance which I have caused My people Yisrael to inherit.168Yirmiyahu 12:14. This is the sense of the expression mentioned here, as Yisrael ‘did’ unto the Land of his inheritance,169Verse 12. This would seem to indicate that at the time that Esav conquered his land, Yisrael had already conquered theirs. But Yisrael had, at that time, not taken possession of any land. when it was not yet done! [But the meaning thereof is as explained: that just as G-d would be wroth with him who would rob Yisrael of his inheritance after He will have given it to him, in the same way, He does not give Yisrael the right to take the land of Esav after having given it to him.]
Similarly He further said with reference to [the land of] the children of Amon that it is of the land of the Refaim [which G-d gave to Avraham]170Genesis 15:20. for that, too, belonged first to the Refaim. Bnei Amon called them Zamzumim,171Further, Verse 20. from the expression ‘z’mamo (his evil scheme) do not further,172Psalms 140:9. except that [the letters zayin and mem] are doubled [in the name “Zamzumim”], which thus indicates “the people from whom nothing is withheld which they purpose to do.”173See Genesis 11:6.

Teichasheiv’ (accounted). The land of Amon, too, is considered part of the land of Refaim; in other words, it is included within it. Similarly, from the Shichor, which is before Mitzrayim, even unto the border of Ekron northward ‘teichasheiv’ (is accounted) to the Kenaani.174Yehoshua 13:3. So also, the sons of Rimon the Be'eroti, of the children of Binyamin; for Be'erot also ‘teichasheiv’ (is accounted) to Binyamin.175II Shmuel 4:2. It is possible that such is also the meaning of the expression written above [with reference to Moav], these also are ‘yeichashvu’ Refaim,176Above, Verse 11. Scripture stating that the Eimim who formerly dwelled there177See ibid., Verse 10. are also “accounted”178In Verse 10 above Ramban explained yeichashvu as an expression of importance and esteem. Here Ramban explains it as “accounted” [to the Refaim]. Refaim since they were part of them, and they were as the Anakim,176Above, Verse 11. and therefore they [the Moavim] called them ‘Eimim’176Above, Verse 11. [because their “dread,” like that of the Anakim (giants) lay upon the people]. This is the correct interpretation.
Thus the land of Refaim was very large, and from it, Moav and Amon took their lands. The balance remained for the Refaim themselves, for Og, who dwelled in Ashtarot, was of them, as is stated, and they smote the Refaim in Ashteroth-karnaim.155Ibid., Verse 5. And in the Book of Yehoshua it is written, and cut down a space for thyself there in the land of the Perizi and of the Refaim.179Yehoshua 17:15. Therefore, Scripture says of the border of Moav and Amon that it is “accounted to the Refaim,” [still calling them “Refaim,” the name by which they were originally known]. The Moavim and Bnei Amon were the ones that changed [the name of the Refaim] to other names: [the Moavim calling them] Eimim and [Bnei Amon calling them] Zamzumim.

And the Avim that dwelt in villages. Scripture is stating of the Avim that dwelt in villages — without a wall around them180Leviticus 25:31. as far as Azah which was the Kenaani border, as it is said, And the border of the Kenaani was from Zidon, as thou goest toward Gerar, unto Azah181Genesis 10:19. — the Kaftorim that came forth out of Kaftor destroyed them and they dwelt in their stead. Now the Kaftorim were descendants of Mitzraim182Ibid., Verses 13-14. and their land was not part of the gift given to Avraham; nevertheless their land was possessed by Yisrael because the Kaftorim had conquered it from the children of Kenaan. The verse stating with reference to the land of the Plishtim, for unto thee [Yitzchak], and unto thy seed, I will give all these lands183Ibid., 26:3. was said for this reason: that the land [of the Plishtim] originally belonged to the children of Kenaan. Therefore, in the days of Yehoshua Yisrael drove out the five lords of the Plishtim: the Gazite, the Ashdodite, the Ashkelonite, the Giti, and the Ekroni; also the Avim,184Yehoshua 13:3. for they all dwelled within the Kenaani border — in Azah, Ashkelon, Ashdod, and in Ekron. They [the lords] were called by the name of their place [i.e., the Gazite, the Ashdodite etc. because, although they were foreigners, after their conquest of these five Kenaani towns, they adopted their names], for they destroyed the Avim who were of the children of Kenaan185Ramban will later explain that the Avim are identical with the Chivi, and of the Chivi it is clearly written that they were of the children of Kenaan (Genesis 10:17). who dwelled within the border of the Kenaani from Zidon, as thou goest toward Gerar, unto Azah,181Genesis 10:19. and they abode in their stead. Zidon also belonged to the Plishtim, as it is written, And also what are ye to Me, O Tzor, and Zidon, and all the regions of Peleshet?186Yoel 4:4.
In my opinion the Avim are identical with the Chivi [who were of the children of Kenaan],187Genesis 10:15-17. for such is the customary way of Scripture to alter names, as we have said, so long as they indicate the same meaning, and “the serpent”188Indicated by the name Chivim (the Chivi), which is of the term chivah — a snake. ye’aveit (curves) itself.189This suggests the name Avim. Thus the Chivim are identical with the Avim, as both names suggest the snake and its characteristic of crawling crookedly. And in Bereshith Rabbah [we find the following text]:190Bereshith Rabbah 26:17. “Said Rabbi Elazar the son of Rabbi Shimon: They were as expert in [tasting] earth [to determine which crops it is capable of producing] as the serpent [whose only food is the earth]. In the Galil they call chivya (a serpent) ivya.” The Sages used to call it achna,191Berachoth 19. and also chachina.192So found in Aruch Hashalem, under the term chachan that such was the reading in the Talmud. Thus it is clear that the letters a’yin and cheth are interchangeable, which explains why the name “Avim” is identical with “Chivim.” The Rabbis have interpreted:193Vayikra Rabbah 30:3. “‘Vayei’ather’ (and He was entreated) of him, and heard his supplication.194II Chronicles 33:13. Said Rabbi Levi: In Erev they call chatirah (an opening) atirah” [and the meaning of the verse is thus: “and Hashem made ‘an opening’ for his prayer to be accepted”].195The text refers to Menashe, king of Yehudah, who for a long time worshipped the idols. When the Ashur came and carried him off to Bavel and placed him in an oven heated from below, Menashe began calling upon idol after idol to rescue him. When no help came he turned his supplication to Elokim. The attribute of mercy prevented Menashe’s repentance from being accepted because he had lived so wicked a life, but the Holy One, blessed be He, “made an opening” in the Throne of His Glory “and received his prayer” (Sanhedrin 103a). The verse concludes, He brought him back to Yerushalayim into his kingdom. Ramban uses this text to prove that the letter a’yin [in the word vayei’ather — “and He was entreated”] interchanges with the cheth [vayeichather — and He made “an opening”]. This is an additional support to Ramban’s thesis that the Avim are identical with the Chivim — the Chivi. Ramban will go on to cite several further examples of the interchangeability of the letters a’yin and cheth. — In conclusion it should be noted that the episode with Menashe, king of Yehudah, illustrates the efficacy of repentance under all circumstances, for even when all the “gates” were closed to his supplication, Menashe’s prayers were yet accepted through a special “opening” in the “Throne of the Almighty.” The Rabbis have also said:196Eichah Rabbathi 2:2. “How hath Hashem ‘ya’iv’197This is generally explained as being of the word av (a cloud): How hath Hashem ‘covered with a cloud’ … The Midrash will explain it as though it were written with a cheth, as Ramban continues. the daughter of Tziyon in His anger!198Lamentations 2:2. Rabbi Chama the son of Rabbi Chanina explained it as follows: how has Hashem chiyeiv (assigned guilt) in His anger! There are places where they call chiva (guilt) iva.” Chavkim (rungs) are called avkim.199Vayikra Rabbah, 9:1: “The prince of the kingdom of Bavel ascended seventy avkim (rungs).” See also Vol. I, p. 350. Such [interchangeability of the letters a’yin and cheth] is common in the language. Of Rabbi “Chiya” [the Rabbis say],200In this exact form I have not found the source for the statement. However, in Moed Katan 16b, and in Kerithoth 8a we do find Rabbi Chiya being referred to as “Iya.” “And what does ‘Iya’ say of this matter?” Our Rabbis were also accustomed to speak of heisei’ach hada’ath (distractedness or absent-mindedness) instead of hisa hada’ath [changing the a’yin of hisa to cheth of heisei’ach]. In the Talmud Yerushalmi, they always [use the term] hisiya [to signify “distractedness”].201See my Hebrew commentary p. 354, Note 2, for a number of such references. And in the Mishnah we also find:202Tahoroth 7:8. “[If someone was clean] v’heisia (and had given up the thought of) eating.” Commentators have also said of the verse ‘ushu’ and come all ye nations203Yoel 4:11. The commentators referred to, are Menachem ben Saruk and Rashi. that it is like chushu (hasten ye). And in the Mechilta we find:204Mechilta, Pis’cha 7. “Ufasachti,205Exodus 12:13. Rabbi Yashiya says: Do not read ufasachti (and I will protect), but read ufusati (and I will step over), meaning that Elokim, blessed be He, will ‘pass over’ the houses of the children of Yisrael.” He [Rabbi Yashiya] made ufasachti refer to the word p’sioth (steps) by interchanging the cheth with an a’yin.
Scripture now finished informing us about the entire land of the Chivi that was lost [to them]. Part of it was taken by [the children of] Esav206Verse 22. and that is forbidden to us, and part of it was taken by the Kaftorim and we may take it from them.
And in Bereshith Rabbah207Bereshith Rabbah 26:16. I have found that the Avim are identical with Refaim [and not with the Chivi as we have stated hitherto]. Thus the Rabbis comment on the verse, The Nefilim were in the earth:208Genesis 6:4. “The Refaim are the Avim. They were called Refaim [of the root raphoh — weak] because the heart of anyone who beheld them became weak as wax. They were called Avim [of the term ivya — serpent] because they were as expert as a serpent [whose food is the earth] in [tasting] earth [to determine which crops it is capable of producing].” The Rabbis further said there with reference to Elokim’s gift to Avraham:209Bereshith Rabbah 44:27. “Rabbi Dostoie in the name of Rabbi Shmuel said: Because He does not mention here [among the lands of the ten nations given to Avraham] the Chivi, therefore, He introduced the Refaim in their place.” Now when I pondered this text, I found the matter to be true and authentic, correct and affirmed. For Moshe our teacher mentioned to them the seven nations [whose lands] Yisrael inherited, as he said, and He shalt cast out many nations before thee, the Chiti, and the Girgashite, and the Emori, and the Kenaani, and the Perizi, and the Chivi, and the Yevusi, seven nations greater and mightier than thou.210Further, 7:1. Now six of these are mentioned in the gift given to Avraham,211Genesis 15:20-21. but the Chivi is not mentioned there! Then he [the Chivi] must in any case be either the Refaim212Genesis 15:20. or of the Keini, Knizi, and Kadmonite213Ibid., Verse 19. [all of whom are mentioned in the gift to Avraham]. All our Rabbis say209Bereshith Rabbah 44:27. that Yisrael did not inherit [the lands of] the Keini, Knizi and Kadmonite, but that He will make them inherit [those lands] in the future, and about them it is said, And when Hashem thy Elokim enlarge thy boundary, as He hath sworn unto thy fathers, and give thee all the land which He promised to give unto thy fathers.214Further, 19:8. And so also it is not mentioned anywhere that they inherited them in the days of Yehoshua. If so, the Refaim given by Him to Avraham must be the Chivi, who was the sixth son of Kenaan,187Genesis 10:15-17. and who was called Hivi by his father; while in the days of Avraham they surnamed him Refaim. In my opinion the name Refaim is derived from that of the Chivi [Chivi — which as explained above denotes “a serpent”], related to the expression on the lair of the asp and on the viper’s den,215Yeshayahu 11:8. for things that are hidden in the earth [like the serpent], the [Hebrew] language calls ‘rephaim’, for example: ‘ha’rephaim’ (the dead) tremble beneath the waters and the inhabitants thereof;216Iyov 26:5. and the earth shall bring to life ‘rephaim’ (the dead).217Yeshayahu 26:19.
Now the children of this Chivi were very numerous and, when the families of the Kenaani spread abroad,218Genesis 10:18. this family took possession of large territories, some of them called “the land of Refaim;” others, [“the land of] Chori;” and some, [“the land of] Avim;” and generally they were all Chivi, and they were all Refaim, just as, among our people [there are] Efraim, Yehudah, Yisrael — but generally speaking, all are [called] Yisrael. Now, these names [Refaim, Chori, Avim] are all descriptives derived from the name Chivi [Chivi — which denotes “a serpent”] since his name was Chivi they surnamed him Refaim from chivya (a serpent) because the serpent dwells in the holes of the earth [and things that lie hidden in the earth are called “Refaim,” as explained above]. They were likewise called “the Chori” and “the Avim” because of their association with the term serpent, as I have explained above.219Ramban refers to his explanation above that the letters cheth and a’yin interchange. Now since chivya is a snake, the word “Avim” likewise denotes the same. Ramban did not explain the name Chorim (Chori) above; but it is obvious that his intent is that the name is derived from the word chur (a hole), since the serpent dwells in a lair in the ground. Now the Holy One, blessed be He, gave to Avraham [the land of] the Refaim in general,170Genesis 15:20. and Moshe mentioned to Yisrael “the Chivi”210Further, 7:1. which was the first name by which his father [Kenaan] called him,187Genesis 10:15-17. for the land of Refaim was already divided in the days of Moshe and parts of it [i.e., that belonging to Moav, Amon, and the children of Esav] were forbidden to Yisrael. Thus Scripture comes here to mention the subject of the entire land of the Chivi, who are Refaim, and all that was done with it. First it states220Above, Verses 10-11. that the Eimim were also of the Refaim and the Moavim succeeded them. Then it states221Verse 12. that the children of Esav succeeded the Chori, who were also of the Refaim. And then it repeats222Verses 20-21. that the land of Amon was also the land of Refaim, and all this was forbidden to Yisrael. He also narrated223Verse 23. that the Kaftorim who came from Kaftor took part of their land [i.e., of the Avim who are also Refaim] and that [on account of the Kaftorim’s prior conquest] it was permissible for Yisrael. Thus Yehoshua mentioned [to the children of Yosef] the land of the Perizi and of the Refaim224Yehoshua 17:15. [wherein they were to settle].
However, Rashi wrote:225On Verse 23 before us. “The Avim were of the Plishti people,226The Plishtim were descendants of Mitzraim (Genesis 10:14). Thus, while according to Ramban, as explained above, the Avim who are identical with the Chivi and Refaim were descendants of Kenaan whose land was permissible to Yisrael, Rashi holds the Avim to have been part of the Plishtim who were descendants of Mitzraim. Now, both Mitzraim and Kenaan were sons of Cham (ibid., Verse 6). But only the land of the children of Kenaan was given to Avraham. How Rashi’s opinion affects the subject under consideration will be made clear in the text which follows. for they are enumerated together with them in the Book of Yehoshua: [the five lords of the Plishtim:] the Gazite, and the Ashdodite, the Ashkelonite, the Giti, and the Ekroni, also the Avim.184Yehoshua 13:3. But, because of the oath that Avraham had sworn to Avimelech,227Ibid., 21:24. Yisrael could not go into their land to remove them from their territory. Therefore, I brought upon them the Kaftorim and they destroyed them [i.e., the Avim who were Plishtim] and they dwelled in their stead; now you are permitted to take it from them [i.e., the Kaftorim].” But the intent of Rashi’s words are not clear to me. For Scripture [in the verse from Yehoshua quoted above]184Yehoshua 13:3. does not enumerate the Avim among the Plishtim; instead it refers to the five lords of the Plishtim184Yehoshua 13:3. and lists them — and then mentions the Avim as a separate people. The verse states that from the Shichor, which is before Mitzrayim, even unto the border of Ekron northward184Yehoshua 13:3. — all this is accounted the land of Kenaan; [the lands of] the five lords of the Plishtim that it lists, with the Avim who are another people. But according to the Rabbi [Rashi] the land of the Avim became permissible to Yisrael because the Kaftorim had taken it from them, but who made permissible [the lands of] the other lords of the Plishtim?228But according to Ramban, as explained at the beginning of this verse, the Plishtim had taken their land from the children of Kenaan, all of whose lands were given to Avraham. Since the Avim [identical with the Chivi who is mentioned in Genesis 10:17 as a son of Kenaan] were one of the ten children of Kenaan, it is self-understood that their land was permissible to Yisrael. Verse 23 here, telling that the Kaftorim [who were of the children of Mitzraim, like the Plishtim — Genesis 10:14] destroyed the Avim, serves the purpose of informing Yisrael that they should not be misled into thinking that the land is forbidden to them because the Kaftorim were not descended from Kenaan. Therefore, the verse informs us that the Kaftorim had taken it from the Avim who are Kenaani and, consequently, their land is permissible to Yisrael. The same was true of the five lords of the Plishtim who had taken the land away from the Kenaani; hence Yehoshua was permitted to take it from them. All this explains Ramban’s interpretation. Rashi, however, wrote that the Avim were part of the Plishti people, and Verse 23 before us informs us that their land was made permissible to Yisrael because the Kaftorim had taken it from them. On this Ramban asks: if so, what made the lands of the five lords of the Plishtim permissible to Yisrael? There are other questions as well, which Ramban raises on Rashi’s interpretation. And why did Bnei Yisrael conquer all of them, for Yehoshua was the one who suppressed the Plishtim and the Avim! Moreover, [according to Rashi] why should the land of the Plishtim belong to Avraham altogether and why did Avimelech find it necessary to make his covenant [with Avraham]227Ibid., 21:24. in this matter, when the Plishtim are of the children of Mitzraim,229Genesis 10:13-14. and so were the Kaftorim,229Genesis 10:13-14. and they were not of the ten nations [given to Avraham]?230Ibid., 15:19-21. — The question on Rashi is thus made all the stronger: If the Avim and the Kaftorim were Plishtim, why should the land of the Avim have become permissible to Yisrael as a result of its conquest by the Kaftorim? Whichever of the two held the land, it was a Plishti possession and Peleshet was not permissible to Yisrael. But the [fact of the] matter is the opposite! For the Kaftorim and the Plishtim [children of Mitzraim] destroyed the Kenaani, as indicated by the fact that Avimelech [a Plishti, not a Kenaani] was the king of Gerar, [indicating that the Kenaani had been driven out],231Ibid., 20:2. and the Gazite dwelled in Azah, and Zidon was a Plishti city. All these were part of the Kenaani territories, as it is said, And the border of the Kenaani was from Zidon, as thou goest toward Gerar, unto Azah.232Ibid., 10:19.
Now it appears to me that the Plishtim and Kaftorim [children of Mitzraim] were considered one people, and so Scripture states, For Hashem will spoil the Plishtim, the remnant of the isle of Kaftor.233Yirmiyahu 47:4. And this is the sense of the expression [in the verse before us], the Kaftorim that came forth out of Kaftor. It was out of Kaftor that a small [band of] people came forth to sojourn where they could find a place.234Judges 17:8. They destroyed the Avim who were of the seed of Kenaan that dwelled as far as Azah, and the Kaftorim dwelled in their stead in Azah, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Gat, and Ekron — all these places being within the borders of the land of Kenaan and they divided it among their five lords. The name of these districts was Peleshet and they were called Plishtim. The Avim were left with the remainder of their land as Yehoshua mentioned.235This refers to Yehoshua 13:3 [quoted above] where, after mentioning the five lords of the Plishtim, he cites ‘also the Avim.’ According to Ramban this indicates that the Plishtim [who are identical with the Kaftorim, as explained] took but part of the land of the Avim [as stated in Verse 23 before us] while the Avim were still left with part of their land. Now, since the Avim are identical with the Chivi who were of the children of Kenaan, Yehoshua was permitted to take the entire original land of the Avim — what had been conquered by the five lords of the Plishtim, as well as what was still in the hands of the Avim. It is this which is meant by the verse the Plishtim, the remnant of the isle of Kaftor,233Yirmiyahu 47:4. for the Kaftorim were Plishtim. This is also the meaning of the expression, whence went forth the Plishtim and the Kaftorim,236Genesis 10:14. as I have explained there.237Ibid., Vol. I, pp. 149-150. As to what Scripture states, Have I not brought up Yisrael out of Mitzrayim, and the Plishtim from Kaftor, and Aram from Kir?238Amos 9:7. — [which would seem to indicate that the Plishtim were a separate nation that was redeemed from Kaftor just as Yisrael was a separate nation that was redeemed from Mitzrayim — thus contradicting Ramban’s thesis that the Plishtim and the Kaftorim were one nation — the explanation is as follows:] The verse there is speaking of the wars of Hashem. It was He Who brought up Yisrael from the land of Mitzrayim by signs, and by wonders, and by war,239Further, 4:34. and He brought up the Plishtim from Kaftor, their land, because He brought them forth from there, to deliver unto them the Avim through a great miracle and they destroyed them, and dwelt in their stead [as stated in Verse 23 before us] and they left the land of Kaftor to their brothers.240Thus it is again established that the Kaftorim are identical with the Plishtim, as they were one people. Or the matter may have been as I have mentioned, that the Avim, the children of Kenaan who first dwelled in the land, were known as Plishtim because the name of the land was Peleshet. When the Kaftorim that came forth out of Kaftor subdued them, they exiled some of them to their land Kaftor which was part of the land of Mitzrayim, settling them among their brothers [the Kaftorim]. Elokim redeemed them [i.e., the Avim who were known as Plishtim] from there and they returned to their original place [in the land of Kenaan]. We know not in which generation this happened. Thus the Plishtim were inhabitants of the land of Kenaan, and, therefore, Scripture states, The word of Hashem is against you, O Kenaan, the land of the Plishtim; I will even destroy thee, that there shall be no inhabitant.241Tzefanyah 2:5. And so Yisrael did not drive out the Plishtim until the time of the oath had expired, when three generations242The oath was specifically limited to three generations: Now therefore swear unto me here by Elokim that thou [Avraham] wilt not deal falsely with me, nor with my son, nor with my son’s son (Genesis 21:23). of Plishtim in that land of Avimelech had died. And so the Rabbis have said in the Midrash:243Tanchuma, Beshalach 1. “For that was ‘near,’244Exodus 13:17. [meaning] the oath which Avraham had sworn to Avimelech was yet ‘near’ [i.e., was still in effect, because] his grandson was still living” [and therefore Elokim did not lead the people through Peleshet after the exodus from Mitzrayim]. This is a fitting and correct interpretation of this subject.
However, in the Gemara [of Tractate Chullin] in the Chapter V’eilu Treifoth245“These are accounted treifah” among cattle. It is the third chapter of Tractate Chullin. The text quoted is on 60b. the Rabbis have cited an opinion in a dispute agreeing with the words of Rashi [that the Avim were Plishtim]. Rav246Rav, the leading teacher in the first generation of Amoraim in Bavel, laid the foundation for the great Yeshivoth in Bavel. He was a pupil of Rabbi Yehudah Hanasi, also called Rabbeinu Hakadosh, the redactor of the Mishnah in Eretz Yisrael. Rav returned to his native Bavel where he founded the Academy of Sura which existed for about eight hundred years without interruption. His real name was Abba, but because of the great respect accorded to him he was called “Rav,” as Rabbi Yehudah Hanasi was called simply “Rabbi.” said there that the Avim came from Teiman, and we learned a Beraitha247See Vol. II, p. 133, Note 209. that concurs with him. Teiman is of the seed of Edom, as it is written, Of Edom, thus said Hashem of hosts: Is wisdom no more in Teiman?248Yirmiyahu 49:7. This is possible, and, [if so] Scripture is stating of the Avim, who are of the children of Esav, [that] part of their land was made permissible [to Yisrael] through the Kaftorim [who took it from the Avim], just as [parts of the lands of] Amon and Moav were made permissible by Sichon [conquering them]. And what I have written is good and upright.

Behold, I have given into thy hand Sichon. This statement is the same as the one stated below, Behold, I have begun to deliver up Sichon.249Further, Verse 31. Before that, Moshe sent to him [Sichon] messengers out of the wilderness of Kedemot,250Verse 26. Ramban is thus stating that Verses 26-29 [recording Moshe’s proposal for a peaceful passage through Sichon’s land] actually took place before Elokim’s command to him to begin the battle against Sichon as stated in Verse 24. but after Elokim had commanded him, [Moshe, in Verse 24 before us,] begin to possess it, and contend with him in battle he would no longer send him words of peace, saying: ‘Let me pass through thy land.’251Verses 26-27. For if Sichon were to hearken to him, Moshe would have been transgressing the words of Elokim [by not waging war against Sichon as he had been commanded in Verse 24], and if Moshe knew in advance that Sichon would not hearken, his message would have been pointless. [Therefore, we must say that Moshe’s message to Sichon, as stated in Verses 26-29, was sent before Elokim’s command here in Verse 24.] Now, do not think of saying [that Moshe’s message of peace] is in accordance with the commandment wherein we have been charged, When thou drawest nigh unto a city to fight against it, then proclaim peace unto it252Further, 20:10. [and, therefore, you might think that even after Elokim told Moshe to begin to possess Sichon’s land he was still obligated to send the message of peace, here recorded in Verses 26-29 — that is not the case]. For [in the injunction to call for peace] it is written, And it shall be, if it make thee answer of peace, and open unto thee, then it shall be, that all the people that are found therein shall become tributary unto thee, and shall serve you.253Ibid., Verse 11. Here, however, if Sichon had hearkened to them, they would not have touched him at all. But the meaning of the expression, and I sent messengers,250Verse 26.
